```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
# Every chunk on this page runs from the root of the site, whose data/ folder
# holds the same files as that of the workspace, so that the paths read exactly
# as they do in the workspace: data/housing_original.csv.
knitr::opts_knit$set(root.dir = "..")
```

The route taken by the data of the Housing and racial bias case study, from the file deposited by the original authors to the file on which the exercises in the course run, is the subject of this part of the [companion curriculum](index.qmd). In the experiment, presented in full on the [background page](../background.qmd), the original authors emailed public housing authorities across the United States from six names meant to indicate a white, a Black or a Hispanic applicant and coded the replies that came back [@EinsteinGlick2017DoesRaceAffect]. The [module on data sources](data-sources.qmd#sec-dataverse) ends with the deposited file on your disk, checked against the checksum published by the Harvard Dataverse, and the present module starts at that point, working step by step through `R/01_email_data.R`, the first script in the case-study pipeline. It describes each column of the course file, shows how the names, the replies, the greeting codes, the bounced emails and the community thirds are derived, and presents the checks that a rebuilt file has to pass before anything is estimated from it.

The code on the page runs on `housing_original.csv`, the deposited file saved as plain text with its original column names, which the course supplies in its workspace and in `data/`. As every chunk reads the files as the workspace does, each line can be copied into the workspace as it stands, and every number on the page was computed from the file when the page was built.

## 1. Two files {#sec-two-files}

The deposit holds the data as a Stata file, `HousingAuditAJPSFinalPublic_Unidentified.dta`, in which `NumberAssignment` and the six thirds have value labels (the text attached to each code, such as "Brett" for 5 and "Top Third" for 3) and each column has a variable label describing it. The pipeline reads that file with haven and writes it out again with no change to any value or row, in order that anyone without Stata can open it. This step, which is all that separates the two versions of the deposited data, is shown here without being run, because the Stata file is not part of the course repository.

```{r}
#| label: from-stata
#| eval: false
raw <- haven::read_dta("data-raw/dataverse_1HOVTU/HousingAuditAJPSFinalPublic_Unidentified.dta")

original <- raw |>
  dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(dplyr::where(haven::is.labelled), \(x) as.numeric(x))) |>
  haven::zap_label() |>
  haven::zap_formats()
readr::write_csv(original, "data/housing_original.csv", na = "")
```

`as.numeric()` on a labelled column retains the codes and drops the labels, and `zap_label()` and `zap_formats()` remove the variable labels and the Stata display formats. The labels are not lost, since the [codebook of the deposited file](../data/housing_original_codebook.md) records what every code means. Before the data are read, it is worth knowing that the Stata file labels `HispanicEmailer` "Hard to find email address", a copy error in the source, while the original authors' codebook describes the column as recording whether the official who replied had a Hispanic name.

The course holds two files of the same 1,014 emails, in the same order. `housing_original.csv` retains the names and codes given by the original authors, because the reproduction of Task 3 starts from the data as they were published, while `housing_emails.csv`, the course file rebuilt from the deposited one in the rest of this page, gives every column a readable name and adds the columns used in the exercises.

## 2. Reading the deposited file {#sec-reading}

The file is read with readr, a choice that matters for this file in particular, because the replies carry text in `WaitListFinal`, and readr reads an empty cell as a missing value (`NA`), whereas `datawizard::data_read()` returns some of the empty cells in this column as empty strings rather than as missing values.

```{r}
#| label: read-original
original <- readr::read_csv("data/housing_original.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

dplyr::glimpse(original)
```

The file holds `r format(nrow(original), big.mark = ",")` rows, one for each email, and `r ncol(original)` columns. Three of the columns describe the email before it was sent: `NumberAssignment`, the email account from which it was sent, `TreatmentGroup`, the same assignment as text, and `HardEmail`, whether the address had to be taken from the list of housing authorities kept by the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) because the authority offered no contact that could be found quickly. Five record what came back: `Response_Dichotomous`, `Respond24`, `ProperName`, `HispanicEmailer` and `WaitListFinal`. The remaining six contain the five community thirds and the third of the authority on the HUD assessment score, to which section 6 returns.

## 3. The names {#sec-names}

As the file records the name that signed each email only through the number of the account, the first step of the build is a key that translates the six numbers into the name, the group that the name was meant to indicate and the sex of the name. The key is taken from the original authors' codebook, and the paper names the six senders: Brett Smith and Emily Smith, Tyrone Johnson and Shanice Johnson, Santiago Martinez and Gabriela Martinez.

```{r}
#| label: names-key
names_key <- tibble::tibble(
  NumberAssignment = 1:6,
  name = c("Tyrone", "Shanice", "Santiago", "Gabriela", "Brett", "Emily"),
  group = c("black", "black", "hispanic", "hispanic", "white", "white"),
  name_sex = c("male", "female", "male", "female", "male", "female")
)
```

A key typed by hand is arguably the most likely place for an error in the whole build, and the deposited file offers a way to check it. `TreatmentGroup` records the same assignment as `NumberAssignment` in words, and the original authors' codebook calls the column redundant, which is precisely what makes it useful here. Joining the key to the file and cross-tabulating the two should put every email of each name in a single cell of the text column:

```{r}
#| label: names-check
original |>
  datawizard::data_join(names_key, join = "left", by = "NumberAssignment") |>
  datawizard::data_tabulate(select = "TreatmentGroup", by = "name") |>
  insight::print_md()
```

Each name falls in the cell of its own group and sex, and nowhere else, which shows that the key agrees with the text written by the original authors. The six names were sent between `r min(table(original$NumberAssignment))` and `r max(table(original$NumberAssignment))` times. A swap of two names within one group, Santiago for Gabriela, say, would leave every count by group intact, and the cross-tabulation against the text column is the only check on the page that would catch it.

## 4. The columns of the course file {#sec-columns}

The rest of the build is one pipe, taken almost line for line from `01_email_data.R`. The pipe numbers the emails, converts empty text into missing values, joins the key, selects the columns in the order of the course file under their new names, and turns the codes of the community thirds into labelled categories.

```{r}
#| label: build
housing <- original |>
  datawizard::data_modify(email_id = 1:n(), WaitListFinal = datawizard::convert_to_na(WaitListFinal, na = "")) |>
  datawizard::data_join(names_key, join = "left", by = "NumberAssignment") |>
  datawizard::data_select(c(
    "email_id", "name", "group", "name_sex",
    hard_email = "HardEmail",
    reply = "Response_Dichotomous",          # missing = the email bounced
    reply24 = "Respond24",                   # replies only
    named = "ProperName",                    # replies only; 5 replies uncoded
    hispanic_official = "HispanicEmailer",   # replies only
    waitlist = "WaitListFinal",
    white_third = "white_pop_third",
    black_third = "black_pop_third",
    hispanic_third = "hispanic_pop_third",
    pop_third = "total_pop_third",
    poverty_third = "poverty_pop_third",
    assessment_third = "assesment_third"
  )) |>
  datawizard::data_modify(
    .at = c("white_third", "black_third", "hispanic_third", "pop_third", "poverty_third", "assessment_third"),
    .modify = \(x) factor(x, levels = 1:3, labels = c("lower", "middle", "top"))
  )
```

`data_select()` renames as it selects, with the new name on the left of each pair and the old one on the right, the order of the vector thus being the order of the columns in the result. `convert_to_na()` matters when the source is the Stata file, in which an empty text cell arrives as an empty string, whereas the column read from the CSV by readr holds no empty strings, and there the line changes nothing. The pipeline retains the line in order that the build yields the same file from either source. The sixteen columns of the result are listed in the table below, with the source of each.

| Column | What it holds | From |
|:--|:--|:--|
| `email_id` | The row number of the email, 1 to 1,014, which orders the rows and identifies nothing outside the file | the row order |
| `name`, `group`, `name_sex` | The name that signed the email, the group that it was meant to indicate (`white`, `black`, `hispanic`) and its sex | `NumberAssignment` and the key |
| `hard_email` | 1 if the address came from the list kept by HUD, 0 if the authority gave an address or a contact form | `HardEmail` |
| `reply` | 1 if the authority replied, 0 if not, missing if the email bounced | `Response_Dichotomous` |
| `reply24` | Replies only: 1 if the reply came within 24 hours | `Respond24` |
| `named` | Replies only: 1 if the reply opened with the name of the sender, in any form | `ProperName` |
| `hispanic_official` | Replies only: 1 if the official who replied had a distinctively Hispanic name | `HispanicEmailer` |
| `waitlist` | Replies only, as text: the wait in months, `Closed` or `No Housing` | `WaitListFinal` |
| `white_third` … `poverty_third` | The third of the community, among the communities of the study, on percent white, percent Black, percent Hispanic, population and the poverty rate | the five `_pop_third` columns |
| `assessment_third` | The third of the housing authority on the HUD assessment score | `assesment_third` |

The counts of every column and the notes on its coding are given in the [codebook of the course file](../data/housing_emails_codebook.md).

## 5. Replies, greetings and bounced emails {#sec-outcomes}

The columns that describe a reply are missing by design wherever there was no reply, and the pattern of their missing values is itself part of the data. `reply` is missing for an email that bounced, which never reached an official. The four columns that describe a reply exist only for the emails that drew one, and `named` is missing as well for the replies whose greeting was not coded by the original authors. A rebuilt file should show exactly this pattern, the counts reported on the [background page](../background.qmd) serving as the test.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-counts
#| tbl-cap: "The emails of the Housing case study by the group of the name: sent, bounced (no reply status), delivered, replied, replied with a greeting code, and opened with the name of the sender. Source: `data/housing_original.csv`, rebuilt on this page."
counts <- housing |>
  datawizard::data_summary(
    Sent = n(), Bounced = sum(is.na(reply)), Delivered = sum(!is.na(reply)),
    Replied = sum(reply %in% 1), Coded = sum(!is.na(named)), Named = sum(named %in% 1),
    by = "group"
  )
counts |>
  datawizard::data_rename(select = c(Group = "group")) |>
  tinytable::tt() |>
  tinytable::style_tt(j = 2:7, align = "r")
```

```{r}
#| label: count-totals
#| include: false
totals <- housing |>
  datawizard::data_summary(sent = n(), bounced = sum(is.na(reply)), delivered = sum(!is.na(reply)),
                           replied = sum(reply %in% 1), coded = sum(!is.na(named)))
```

Of the `r format(totals$sent, big.mark = ",")` emails, `r totals$bounced` bounced and `r totals$delivered` were delivered, and of the `r totals$replied` that drew a reply, `r totals$replied - totals$coded` carry no greeting code, leaving `r totals$coded` coded replies. The same counts are reported on the background page and in the [codebook](../data/housing_emails_codebook.md#rows-and-missing-values). The pattern behind these counts can be checked directly, by confirming that no email without a reply, bounced or not, carries any value in the columns that describe a reply.

```{r}
#| label: reply-columns
housing |>
  datawizard::data_filter(!(reply %in% 1)) |>
  datawizard::data_select(c("reply24", "named", "hispanic_official", "waitlist")) |>
  is.na() |>
  all()
```

The analyses in the course run on the rows chosen from the file for each question, a choice made through three decisions in the [specification menu](../menu.qmd#level-measurement). Bounced emails are left out under every option, because no official read a bounced email. The emails counted are either the coded replies, the rows of the claim, or all delivered emails, in which case an email without a reply counts as one without a named greeting. The five uncoded replies, finally, are either left out or counted as replies that did not open with the name. The chunk below computes the share of named greetings for white and Hispanic names in the first two ways, with the uncoded replies left out.

```{r}
#| label: two-populations
housing |>
  datawizard::data_filter(!is.na(reply), group %in% c("white", "hispanic")) |>
  datawizard::data_modify(named_any = dplyr::if_else(reply == 0, 0, named)) |>
  datawizard::data_summary(among_replies = 100 * mean(named, na.rm = TRUE),
                           among_delivered = 100 * mean(named_any, na.rm = TRUE),
                           by = "group")
```

```{r}
#| label: population-gaps
#| include: false
pop_shares <- housing |>
  datawizard::data_filter(!is.na(reply), group %in% c("white", "hispanic")) |>
  datawizard::data_modify(named_any = dplyr::if_else(reply == 0, 0, named)) |>
  datawizard::data_summary(among_replies = 100 * mean(named, na.rm = TRUE),
                           among_delivered = 100 * mean(named_any, na.rm = TRUE),
                           by = "group")
gap_replies <- diff(pop_shares$among_replies[match(c("white", "hispanic"), pop_shares$group)])
gap_delivered <- diff(pop_shares$among_delivered[match(c("white", "hispanic"), pop_shares$group)])
```

Since `named` is missing for every email without a reply, `mean(named, na.rm = TRUE)` over the delivered emails corresponds to the share among the coded replies, and the gap between the two groups is `r insight::format_value(gap_replies, digits = 1, style_negative = "minus")` points, the reference specification of the course. `named_any` sets a missing reply to 0 and retains the code of every reply, its mean thus corresponding to the share of all delivered emails, uncoded replies aside, that drew a reply opening with the name, with a gap of `r insight::format_value(gap_delivered, digits = 1, style_negative = "minus")` points. Both numbers are stored in `display_outcomes.csv`, and the [module on audit experiments](experiments.qmd#sec-posttreatment) explains why the two comparisons answer different questions. The helper `spec_frame()` in the course estimator builds the rows of each specification in exactly this way, while the [missing-values module](missingness.qmd) examines what each of the three decisions does to the estimate.

## 6. The community thirds {#sec-thirds}

The public file gives the size, the composition and the poverty of each community, and the assessment score of each authority, only as thirds, coded 1 for the lower, 2 for the middle and 3 for the top third, of the distribution that each measure takes among the communities in the study. The reason, as explained in the ReadMe of the deposit, is that the census codes and the continuous values would identify the housing authorities, and that whether an authority replied to an applicant from a minority is sensitive information. The build turns the codes into a factor with the labels `lower`, `middle` and `top`, in that order, which leads a model or a table to treat the thirds as categories in their natural order and to print the labels.

```{r}
#| label: thirds
housing |>
  datawizard::data_tabulate(select = c("hispanic_third", "poverty_third", "assessment_third")) |>
  insight::print_md()
```

Each community third holds 333 or 334 emails in each band, as a division into thirds should, with the exception of the poverty third, while the assessment third holds fewer emails in its bands because `r sum(is.na(housing$assessment_third))` emails lack it. The community thirds are missing for `r sum(is.na(housing$pop_third))` emails, and the next check shows that these are the same emails for all five thirds, since each email lacks either none of the five thirds or every one of them.

```{r}
#| label: thirds-missing
housing |>
  datawizard::data_select(c("white_third", "black_third", "hispanic_third", "pop_third", "poverty_third")) |>
  datawizard::row_count(count = NA) |>
  datawizard::data_tabulate() |>
  insight::print_md()
```

The original authors do not say why these authorities lack the thirds, and the course does not guess. What the missing values do to the adjusted specifications, which need the thirds, is one of the questions examined in the [missing-values module](missingness.qmd#sec-covariates).

`waitlist` retains the text of the source, in which fewer than half of the entries are numbers of months, often converted by the original authors from phrases such as "two years", the rest being the words `Closed` and `No Housing`. As turning the column into numbers would lose the words, the course file keeps the text, and the [R module](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds/tools/r.html#sec-figure) on the AR4DS site shows how the numeric entries are extracted from it for a figure.

## 7. Checking the rebuilt file {#sec-checks}

A rebuilt file is ready for analysis only when it passes checks written down in advance, and the pipeline stops if any of them fails. `stopifnot()` does nothing when every condition holds and stops at the first condition that does not, which means that a file differing from the counts reported on the background page cannot slip through unnoticed.

```{r}
#| label: stopifnot
stopifnot(
  nrow(housing) == 1014,
  sum(is.na(housing$reply)) == 23,
  sum(housing$reply == 1, na.rm = TRUE) == 563,
  sum(housing$reply == 1 & is.na(housing$named), na.rm = TRUE) == 5,
  all(is.na(housing$named[housing$reply %in% 0])),
  sum(is.na(housing$pop_third)) == 14,
  sum(is.na(housing$assessment_third)) == 344
)
```

The first five conditions are those of `01_email_data.R`, the last two adding the missing thirds. The final check compares the rebuilt file with the course file line by line, as text, which is how the pipeline writes it:

```{r}
#| label: compare
rebuilt_lines <- readr::format_csv(housing, na = "") |> strsplit("\n") |> unlist()
shipped_lines <- readLines("data/housing_emails.csv")
c(rebuilt = length(rebuilt_lines), shipped = length(shipped_lines),
  differing = sum(rebuilt_lines != shipped_lines))
```

Every one of the `r format(length(shipped_lines), big.mark = ",")` lines, the header included, is the same in both. The comparison runs on lines rather than on a checksum of the two files because Git on Windows can be set to rewrite line endings when it puts a file on your disk (the setting `core.autocrlf`), with the result that a checkout of the course may differ byte for byte from the repository while holding exactly the same lines. The pipeline ends by writing the file, with an empty cell for every missing value, as the deposited file has:

```{r}
#| label: write
#| eval: false
readr::write_csv(housing, "data/housing_emails.csv", na = "")
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try it

Change the key so that code 3 reads `Gabriela` and code 4 `Santiago`, rerun the build, and note which of the checks on the page fail and which still pass. Then add `named_any` to the course file as a column of its own, with a comment that names its source columns, and compute the share for each of the six names; compare the result with `named_all_pct` in `display_names.csv`, which counts the uncoded replies differently, and work out from its [codebook](../data/displays_codebook.md) why the two can differ for some names. Finally, write one more condition for `stopifnot()` that would catch a reply recorded for a bounced email.
:::

## Sources {#sec-sources}

The data come from the replication package deposited by the original authors [@EinsteinGlick2017DoesRaceAffect] on the Harvard Dataverse ([doi:10.7910/DVN/1HOVTU](https://doi.org/10.7910/DVN/1HOVTU)) and dedicated to the public domain under CC0, a package whose ReadMe explains the blinding of the community values and whose codebook explains the coding of every column. The script followed on this page is `R/01_email_data.R`, and the order of the pipeline is given in `R/README.md`. The two files are documented in the codebooks of the [deposited file](../data/housing_original_codebook.md) and of the [course file](../data/housing_emails_codebook.md). The route of the deposited file from the Dataverse to your disk is described in the [module on data sources](data-sources.qmd#sec-dataverse).
